definition.text: Replication in computing means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent.

facts.text: Replication is a fundamental technique across databases, file systems and distributed systems that improves availability, fault tolerance, accessibility and performance.
With replication, systems keep operating when components fail (failover), serve requests from geographically distributed locations, and balance load across machines.
The challenge is keeping replicas consistent while managing the trade-offs between consistency, availability and network partition tolerance, constraints known as the CAP theorem.
Data replication stores the same data on multiple storage devices; computation replication runs the same task many times, either on separate devices (in space) or repeatedly on one device (in time).
Replication should be transparent to an external user: access to a replicated entity is typically uniform with access to a single one, and a failover of replicas should be hidden as much as possible.
A backup differs from replication: a backup copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.
Replication shares information to keep redundant resources, such as multiple databases, consistent in order to improve reliability, fault tolerance or accessibility.
Database replication improves durability and availability, and copying data across multiple nodes scales read operations while improving redundancy.

definition.text: In single-leader (primary/replica) replication, one database instance is the leader that handles all writes and propagates them to replica nodes.

facts.text: The leader logs its updates, which propagate to replica nodes, and each replica acknowledges receipt of updates.
Replicas primarily serve read requests, but they may serve stale data because of replication lag, the delay in propagating changes from the leader.

In a primary-backup scheme the primary streams a log of updates to a standby backup that takes over if the primary fails; if part of the log is lost, the backup may differ and transactions could be lost.
A weakness of primary-backup is that only one machine is performing operations: fault tolerance is gained, but the identical backup system doubles the costs.
In master-slave replication the master serves reads and writes and replicates writes to one or more slaves, which serve only reads; slaves can replicate further slaves in a tree-like fashion.
If the master goes offline, the system keeps operating in read-only mode until a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned.

Master-slave benefits: backups of the whole database barely affect the master, applications can read from slaves without loading the master, and slaves can go offline and be synced back without downtime.
Master-slave costs: more hardware and complexity, downtime and possible data loss when the master fails, all writes still go to the master, and more read slaves mean more replication lag.

definition.text: Multi-master replication is a method of database replication in which a group of computers stores the data and any member can update it.

facts.text: All members respond to client queries, and the system propagates each member's modifications to the rest of the group and resolves conflicts between concurrent changes made by different members.
In master-slave replication a single master per data item is the only node allowed to modify it; this makes consistency easier to achieve but is less flexible than multi-master replication.
Unlike failover clustering, where passive replicas prepare for takeover and only the master serves clients, every master in a multi-master system is active.

The primary purposes are increased availability and faster server response time: if one master fails the others keep updating, and masters can sit in several physical sites, enabling local write processing across data centers.

The drawbacks are that most systems are only loosely consistent (lazy and asynchronous), eager replication is complex and adds latency, and conflict resolution can become intractable as nodes and latency grow.

Jim Gray argued that unless data splits naturally into disjoint sub-databases, concurrency control conflicts seriously degrade performance, with slowdown possibly scaling as O(n³) in the number of replicas.
In master-master replication both masters serve reads and writes and coordinate with each other; if either goes down, the system keeps serving both reads and writes.

Master-master advantages are reading from both masters, spreading write load and simple, automatic, quick failover; drawbacks are harder setup, loose consistency or higher write latency, and conflict resolution as write nodes and latency grow.

definition.text: When concurrent modifications land on different leader nodes, a replicated database must either prevent the transactional conflict or resolve it afterwards.

facts.text: The most common challenge in multi-master replication is preventing or resolving transactional conflicts when concurrent modifications happen on different leader nodes.
Most synchronous (eager) replication solutions prevent conflicts, while asynchronous (lazy) solutions have to resolve them.

If one record changes on two nodes at once, an eager system detects the conflict before confirming the commit and aborts one transaction; a lazy system lets both commit and resolves the conflict during re-synchronization.
Conflict resolution methods include last-write-wins, application-specific logic and merging concurrent updates.

title: Synchronous and asynchronous replication

definition.text: Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy to acknowledge a write, while asynchronous replication completes the write once local storage acknowledges it.

facts.text: Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss with atomic write operations: a write is not complete until both local and remote storage acknowledge it.

Because most applications wait for the write to complete, synchronous replication lowers overall performance considerably, and performance drops in proportion to distance since minimum latency is set by the speed of light.
For a 10 km distance the fastest possible round trip takes 67 μs, whereas an entire local cached write completes in about 10–20 μs; latency decides how far apart sites can be.

In asynchronous replication a write is complete as soon as local storage acknowledges it and remote storage updates with a small lag, so performance is much higher but the most recent data may be lost if local storage fails.

Semi-synchronous replication counts a write as complete when local storage acknowledges and the remote server receives or logs it; the remote write itself is asynchronous, so durability is not guaranteed on local failure.

The difference between the two is how data is written to the replica: synchronous replication writes to primary storage and the replica simultaneously, so the two copies should always stay synchronized.
Asynchronous replication copies data to the replica after it is already written to primary storage; it can be near-real-time but more commonly runs on a schedule, and it is more cost-effective.

In synchronous database replication a transaction is not committed until all servers have committed it, so failover loses nothing; asynchronous replication allows delay, so transactions might be lost in a failover and replicas may return slightly stale results.

definition.text: Replication lag is the delay in propagating changes from the leader to its replicas, which can leave replicas serving stale data.

facts.text: Under network delay or server overload, replica data might be seconds or even minutes behind the primary.
A user who checks an order right after placing it may hit a lagging replica and not see the order at all, so the setup needs read-after-write consistency.
One mitigation is to send latency-sensitive reads, and reads that immediately follow writes, to the primary database.

Another is to check whether a replica has caught up with the primary, which a relational database generally supports: query the replica if it is up to date, otherwise fail the read or read from the primary.

definition.text: In the read replica pattern, all data-modifying commands go to the primary database and reads go to read replicas.

facts.text: Inserts, deletes and updates are sent to the primary DB and replicated to the read replicas, which serve reads such as viewing order details or order history.
There are two common ways to implement the pattern: embed the routing logic in the application code, or use database middleware.

Database middleware provides transparent routing between the application and the database servers, with rules customizable by user, schema, statement and so on, and acts as a proxy using the standard MySQL network protocol.
Middleware simplifies application code, since the application need not know the database topology, and any MySQL-compatible client can connect, which makes database migration easier.
Middleware adds complexity and network latency, and because all queries go through it, it usually needs a high-availability setup to avoid a single point of failure.

definition.text: Active replication processes the same request at every replica, while passive replication processes each request on one replica and transfers the result to the others.

facts.text: In a primary-backup or primary-replica scheme, one leader replica chosen by leader election processes all requests, a design predominant in high-availability clusters.

In a multi-primary or multi-master scheme any replica can process a request and distribute the new state, so some form of distributed concurrency control, such as a distributed lock manager, is needed.
State machine replication is sometimes mistakenly used as a synonym of active replication.

title: Replication models
article: Replication (computing)#Terminology > Replication models in distributed systems

definition.text: Three widely cited models for data replication are transactional replication, state machine replication and virtual synchrony.

facts.text: Transactional replication, used for replicating transactional data such as a database, follows one-copy serializability: valid outcomes on replicated data accord with ACID.

State machine replication assumes a deterministic finite automaton and atomic broadcast of every event, is based on distributed consensus, and is usually implemented as a replicated log of Paxos rounds.

In virtual synchrony, processes form a group, a joining process receives a checkpoint of the replicated state, and multicasts reach all members in identical order, with membership changes delivered as a new membership view.

definition.text: Chain replication is a family of multi-primary protocols that arrange replicas in a chain for writes to get high throughput and strong consistency.

facts.text: Modern multi-primary replication protocols optimize for the common failure-free operation, and chain replication is a popular family of them.
Chain replication enables local reads on all replica nodes but has high latency for writes, which must traverse several nodes sequentially.
The Hermes protocol combines invalidations and logical timestamps for strong consistency with local reads and high-performance writes from all replicas, committing after one multicast round trip.

definition.text: Databases replicate data changes between nodes by shipping SQL statements, the storage engine's write-ahead log, or row-level changes.

facts.text: Statement-based replication logs write requests such as SQL statements and sends them to replicas for execution, which is problematic with non-deterministic functions or statements with side effects.
Write-ahead log shipping replicates the storage engine's low-level log, which keeps data structures identical across nodes.
Logical (row-based) replication describes changes at the row level in a dedicated log format, giving more flexibility and independence from storage engine internals.

definition.text: Storage replication copies block-device updates to several physical disks, so any file system on top is replicated without modification.

facts.text: It is implemented in hardware, in a disk array controller, or in software, in a device driver.
Disk mirroring is the most basic method and is a local, short-distance operation; replication can extend across a network so disks sit in distant locations.
The purpose is to prevent damage from failures or disasters at one location or to improve the ability to recover data.
Point-in-time replication replicates periodic snapshots of only the changed data, so it can use cheaper bandwidth links such as iSCSI or T1 instead of fiberoptic lines.

definition.text: File-based replication copies data at the logical level of individual files rather than at the storage block level.

facts.text: It relies almost exclusively on software; a kernel filter driver can intercept file system calls such as open, write and delete and send them to another machine, which mimics them.
Like block-level replication it can be synchronous or asynchronous, but synchronous mode is less common for file replication products.
File-level replication can skip data of no business value, such as temporary files, and transmit only what an application wrote, for example 100 bytes instead of a whole 4,096-byte disk block.
Batch replication compares source and destination and makes the destination match; it is generally free or inexpensive, such as rsync, but system-intensive, so it generally runs infrequently.

definition.text: A single point of failure is a part of a system that would stop the entire system from working if it failed.

facts.text: The term implies there is no backup or redundant option that would let the system keep functioning without that part.
A single point of failure is undesirable in any system aiming at high availability or reliability, because its interruption is substantially more disruptive than an error elsewhere in the system.
Systems are made robust by adding redundancy at all potential single points of failure, which are found by identifying the critical components whose malfunction would cause total failure.
In computing, fault tolerance can be achieved at the internal component level, at the system level with multiple machines, or at the site level with replication.
At the system level one normally deploys a load balancer for a server cluster, with spare servers waiting to take on the work of a failed server.
A data center can itself be a single point of failure, so at site level the whole cluster may be replicated at another location, typically as part of an IT disaster recovery program.
Scholars have argued that outsourcing that duplication to cloud providers simply moves the single point of failure and may even raise the likelihood of a failure or cyberattack.
Networks such as the Internet are designed with no single point of failure: multiple paths let packets route around damage after the failure of any one path or intermediate node.

title: Performance bottleneck
article: Single point of failure#Computing > Software engineering

definition.text: A bottleneck occurs when the capacity of an application or computer system is limited by a single component.

facts.text: The bottleneck is the part with the lowest throughput of all parts of the transaction path.
A common example is code that could use parallel processing but runs several independent processes sequentially instead of simultaneously.
Tracking down bottlenecks, or hot spots, is called performance analysis and is done with specialized profilers, with the objective of making those sections of code as fast as possible.
Bottlenecks, like series circuits, are design structures that create single points of failure.

title: Failover

definition.text: Failover is when a standby or replica takes over the work of a failed component so that the system keeps operating.

facts.text: A failover of replicas should be hidden as much as possible from users with respect to quality of service.
In failover clustering, passive replica servers replicate the master's data to prepare for takeover if the master stops functioning, while the master is the only server active for client interaction.
In primary-backup replication, the backup is a standby process that takes over if the primary fails; in master-slave replication, a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned.
In master-master replication failover is simple, automatic and quick, because both masters already serve reads and writes.
At the system level, spare servers can wait to take on the work of a server that fails.
Failover is switching to a redundant or standby computer server, system, hardware component or network when the previously active one fails or terminates abnormally.
In PostgreSQL a standby leaves standby mode and becomes the primary when pg_ctl promote is run, and a warm standby is typically only moments from full availability once activated.

Automatic failover can be dangerous: if a primary cannot tell whether its secondary is healthy, one SRE design has it make itself unavailable and call a human, to avoid split-brain, which protects data but hurts availability and scales poorly.

title: Quorum

definition.text: A quorum is the minimum number of votes a distributed transaction must obtain before it may perform an operation in a distributed system.

facts.text: Quorum-based techniques enforce consistent operation in a distributed system, working both as a replica control method and as a commit method that keeps transactions atomic despite network partitioning.
In replica control each copy holds a vote, and an operation needs a read quorum Vr or write quorum Vw. The rule Vr + Vw > V (V the total votes) makes every read quorum include the newest version.
A second rule ensures two write operations on the same item cannot happen concurrently; together the two rules maintain one-copy serializability.

In Gifford's weighted voting, copies get votes and r + w must exceed the file's total votes so every read quorum overlaps every write quorum; version numbers show which copies are current, and r and w tune reliability and performance.
In commit protocols a transaction runs only if a majority of sites vote for it: a commit quorum Vc is needed to commit and an abort quorum Va to abort, so it cannot commit and abort at once.
A majority quorum keeps a partitioned cluster safe: the sub-partition holding a majority of the votes stays available while the others fall into an auto-fencing mode.

notes: Gifford's 1979 weighted-voting abstract is cited here (one entry at most per paper). The second quorum rule is not printed in the page's sentences (only its purpose), so no formula is given for it.

title: Split-brain

definition.text: Split-brain is a state of data or availability inconsistency caused by two separate data sets with overlapping scope, typically when servers stop communicating and synchronizing, as in a network partition.

facts.text: High-availability clusters watch node health over a private heartbeat link. If all those links fail while the nodes keep running, each node believes it is the only one running.
Each side then serves clients from its own data set with no coordination, which can corrupt data or cause inconsistencies that need operator cleanup.
File servers that watch each other by heartbeat and shoot the other node with STONITH can both take mastership, or both go down, when the network is slow, corrupting data or making it unavailable.
The SRE book's diagnosis: the system solves a leader election problem with simple timeouts, and leader election is a form of distributed consensus that cannot be solved correctly using heartbeats.

Optimistic approaches let partitioned nodes keep working, gaining availability at the cost of correctness and reconciling afterwards; pessimistic approaches give up availability for consistency by limiting access to sub-partitions.
A typical pessimistic approach is quorum consensus: the sub-partition with a majority of the votes stays available and the rest fence themselves off; MongoDB replica sets work this way.
Modern high-availability clusters combine heartbeat connections with quorum witness storage; a two-node cluster without a witness cannot tell which member should be active when the heartbeat fails.
Two replicated file servers must never write simultaneously, because that could corrupt data, possibly unrecoverably. Each pair has a leader and a follower that monitor each other by heartbeats.

notes: Split-horizon DNS (a deliberate, harmless case of the name) was skipped. Facts 3 and 4 come from the SRE book's split-brain case study; the page has no CONTESTED claim.; From the three case studies of Google SRE book chapter 23.

title: Leader election

definition.text: Leader election is the process of designating a single process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes.

facts.text: After a leader election algorithm runs, every node in the network recognizes the same unique node as the leader of the task.
A valid algorithm must terminate in finite time, ensure uniqueness (exactly one process considers itself leader) and agreement (all other processes know who the leader is).
The nodes must break the symmetry among them; with unique, comparable identities they can compare identities and choose the node with the highest identity as leader.

No deterministic algorithm can elect a leader in an anonymous ring, where all processes are identical and run at the same speed, because symmetry cannot be broken; randomized algorithms pick a leader with high probability.

In the Chang and Roberts ring algorithm each processor sends its ID clockwise, passing on bigger IDs and discarding smaller ones, so the highest ID wins, with O(n^2) messages worst case and O(n log n) on average.
Leader election is equivalent to distributed consensus. The SRE book recommends formally proven consensus systems wherever you see leader election, critical shared state or distributed locking.

A highly available service can replicate a simple program and use leader election so only one leader works at a time; a single leader gives coarse mutual exclusion and often coordinates a pool of workers.
In Raft a follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate and starts an election; Paxos can also select a leader, and ZooKeeper offers leader election as a use case.

notes: The ring, mesh, hypercube and radio-network algorithm details were reduced to the ideas an interview needs; Shout, mega-merger and yo-yo (universal techniques for unknown topologies) are only mentioned.

title: Conflict-free replicated data type

definition.text: A conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) is a data structure replicated across computers that any replica can update independently and concurrently, with a built-in algorithm that resolves inconsistencies so replicas converge.

facts.text: Uncoordinated concurrent updates can leave replicas inconsistent in ways that may not be resolvable. Optimistic replication lets all updates through and merges later; CRDTs are the data structures for which that merge always works.
CRDTs are a common way to obtain strong eventual consistency, in two variants: state-based and operation-based.
Development was motivated by collaborative text editing and mobile computing; CRDTs have also been used in online chat, and Redis, Riak and Cosmos DB have CRDT data types.
A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative to operational transformation; known ones include Treedoc, RGA, Woot, Logoot and LSEQ.
League of Legends uses the Riak CRDT implementation for in-game chat with 7.5 million concurrent users and 11,000 messages per second.

notes: Operational transformation has no entry yet (it is the alternative named for collaborative editing); the long industry-use list and history were skipped.

title: State-based and operation-based CRDTs
article: Conflict-free replicated data type#Types of CRDTs

definition.text: State-based CRDTs replicate by sending full state to be merged, while operation-based CRDTs replicate by sending the update operations.

facts.text: State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs) send their full local state to other replicas, which merge it into theirs; the merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent so reordering and duplicated messages do no harm.
Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs) have no merge function: they send update operations, such as +10 or -20, which must be commutative and associative and delivered to each replica without duplication.
State-based CRDTs are simpler to design and need only a gossip protocol from the network, but the whole state must eventually reach every replica; delta CRDTs send only recent changes.

Operation-based CRDTs send small operations, using less bandwidth when transactions are few compared with the state size, but need middleware that never drops or duplicates operations and delivers them in causal order.

title: Common CRDT data types

definition.text: Counters and sets are built as CRDTs by giving each replica its own slot or tag and merging with maximum or union operations.

facts.text: A G-Counter gives each node its own array slot that it increments; replicas merge by taking the maximum of every slot, and the value is the sum of the slots.
A PN-Counter combines two G-Counters, one counting increments and one counting decrements, and its value is the increment total minus the decrement total.
A G-Set only allows adds and merges by union. A 2P-Set adds a tombstone set so elements can be removed, but a removed element can never be added again.

An LWW-Element-Set timestamps each add and remove so the latest wins; an OR-Set tags each add uniquely and removes only the tags it has observed, so an element stays present while any add tag is unremoved.

title: Gossip protocol

definition.text: A gossip or epidemic protocol is a procedure of peer-to-peer communication based on the way epidemics spread.

facts.text: Each node periodically picks another node at random and shares what it knows, so a rumor roughly doubles its reach each round, and the doubling keeps the protocol robust even when some messages are lost.

Typical gossip traits: periodic pairwise interactions, exchanges of bounded size, reliable communication not assumed, a low interaction frequency compared with message latency, random peer selection and implicit redundancy of delivered information.

Dissemination protocols flood information through the network with bounded worst-case load; aggregation protocols compute network-wide values, such as the largest or smallest, using fixed-size pairwise exchanges over rounds logarithmic in system size.
Information reaches all nodes in time logarithmic in system size: in a 25,000-machine network a search string spreads in about 15 rounds and the best match is found after about 30 rounds in all.

Gossip is used to keep distributed databases consistent, count nodes, spread news, build overlay networks, compute aggregates and elect leaders; Dynamo uses a gossip-based membership protocol and failure detection.

Randomized update-distribution algorithms from the 1987 epidemic-algorithms paper are simple, need few guarantees from the communication system, tune cost through the randomization, and ensure every update is eventually reflected in all replicas.
The SRE book warns that ad hoc means such as heartbeats and gossip protocols will always have reliability problems for consensus-type problems like master election and group membership.

notes: The Demers et al. 1987 abstract (paper>10.1145/41840.41841) is OCR-garbled in the corpus; fact 6 paraphrases the legible phrases of its one sentence.

title: Leaderless replication

definition.text: In leaderless replication any replica accepts writes, as in Dynamo, a set of techniques for a highly available key-value store with no distinguished node.

facts.text: Replication can be single-leader, multi-leader or leaderless. Dynamo is leaderless, while DynamoDB, built on Dynamo's principles, uses single-leader replication.

Dynamo's principles: symmetry (every node has the same responsibilities, no special node), decentralization (peer-to-peer over central control), incremental scalability (add one node at a time) and heterogeneity (work proportional to server capability).
It partitions data with consistent hashing, which gives incremental, possibly linear scalability in proportion to the number of collaborating nodes.
For highly available writes it uses vector clocks (or dotted-version-vector sets) and reconciles conflicting versions during reads.
For temporary failures it uses a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, keeping availability and durability when some replicas are unavailable.
For permanent failures it uses anti-entropy with Merkle trees, which finds differences between replica owners so divergent replicas can be synchronized proactively.
Membership and failure detection use a gossip-based protocol, avoiding a central registry of members and node liveness and preserving symmetry.
Cassandra, Project Voldemort and Riak were inspired by the Dynamo paper.

notes: Complements the existing 'Amazon Dynamo' entry (the paper's motivation) with the techniques table from the Wikipedia Dynamo page; no source here explains leaderless replication in general beyond the one naming sentence, so the entry teaches it through Dynamo.

definition.text: Database servers can work together for high availability, by letting a second server take over if the primary fails, or for load balancing, by letting several computers serve the same data.

facts.text: Read-only servers combine easily, but read/write servers are hard: a write to any server must reach all servers so later reads stay consistent. This synchronization problem is the fundamental difficulty, and each solution minimizes it for a specific workload.

Some solutions let only one server modify data: primary servers read and write, standby servers track the primary's changes. A warm standby cannot be connected to until promoted; a hot standby accepts read-only queries.
Solutions differ in granularity: some handle only an entire database server, others allow control per table or per database.
Performance must be weighed in any choice; there is usually a trade-off between functionality and performance.

title: Log-shipping standby servers

definition.text: Log shipping builds a high-availability setup in which a standby server continuously replays the primary's write-ahead log and is ready to take over if the primary fails.

facts.text: Log shipping moves WAL records from one server to another: the primary runs in continuous archiving mode and each standby in continuous recovery mode, reading the WAL files, so the two servers are only loosely coupled.
It needs no changes to database tables, so it has low administration overhead and a relatively low performance impact on the primary compared with some other replication solutions.

File-based shipping sends WAL one 16MB segment at a time, cheaply over any distance, with bandwidth that depends on the primary's transaction rate; record-based shipping streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection.

Log shipping is asynchronous, so transactions not yet shipped are lost if the primary fails. archive_timeout can shrink that window to a few seconds at the cost of bandwidth; streaming replication allows a much smaller one.

A standby is typically moments from full availability once activated, which makes it a warm standby offering high availability; restoring from an archived base backup takes far longer and only gives disaster recovery.
A standby that also serves read-only queries is a hot standby; it applies WAL from the archive, then pg_wal, then streaming from the primary, looping until it is stopped or promoted.
Primary and standby should be as similar as possible: the hardware architecture and major PostgreSQL version must match, and the archive must stay reachable even when the primary is down.

notes: Streaming replication, replication slots, cascading and synchronous replication have their own PostgreSQL pages that were not crawled; setup steps (standby.signal, restore_command) were skipped as administration detail.

title: Logical replication

definition.text: Logical replication replicates data objects and their changes based on their replication identity, usually a primary key, rather than copying physical blocks.

facts.text: Logical replication contrasts with physical replication, which uses exact block addresses and byte-by-byte copying; PostgreSQL supports both, and logical replication allows fine-grained control over data replication and security.
It uses a publish and subscribe model: subscribers pull data from the publications they subscribe to on a publisher node, and may re-publish it to allow cascading or more complex setups.

Replication of a table starts with a snapshot copy to the subscriber, then changes made since the copy are sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, so transactional consistency holds within one subscription.

Use cases include sending incremental changes of a subset of a database, consolidating several databases into one for analytics, replicating between major versions or platforms, and sharing a subset of data between databases.
A read-only subscriber causes no conflicts from a single subscription, but other writes to the same tables, by an application or other subscribers, can cause conflicts.
